alignment.note: Greek and Syriac open with a fronted demonstrative/article (Ὁ / ܗܘ) functioning as the subject anchor before the conjunction; the Vulgate has no separate element here, integrating the subject directly into the proper noun Pilatus. The construction is equivalent but the Latin lacks the resumptive pronoun.

The dative object αὐτοῖς ('to them') is rendered explicitly in the Vulgate (eis) but is absent in the Peshitta clause, which leaves the addressees implicit in the verb of answering. The omission is stylistic and does not alter the sense.

Greek uses a single participle λέγων ('saying') subordinated to the finite verb; both Syriac (ܘܐܡܪ, 'and said') and Latin (et dixit) convert this to a coordinated finite verb introduced by the conjunction, a typical Semitic and Latin parataxis replacing the Greek participial idiom. The Latin colon (:) is included here as discourse punctuation introducing direct speech.
θέλετε / ܨܒܝܢ ܐܢܬܘܢ / Vultis; the Syriac analytically expresses the 2nd-person plural with an enclitic pronoun (ܐܢܬܘܢ), whereas Greek and Latin inflect synthetically.

Greek marks the noun with the accusative article τὸν βασιλέα ('the King'); Syriac ܡܠܟܐ and Latin regem render the noun anarthrously, Syriac having no definite article and Latin no article at all, so the determinacy carried by the Greek article is structurally unexpressed in the other two traditions.
τῶν Ἰουδαίων / ܕܝܗܘܕܝܐ / Judæorum; the interrogative force marked by the Greek and Latin question mark is carried by intonation/context in Syriac.
